label: Differential Geometry of Surfaces
notes: This chapter, printed pages 342 to 365, builds the local measurement kit for a smooth surface in space. We move from a two-parameter patch to the two fundamental forms, then to curvature, principal directions, and Gauss's remarkable theorem that bending leaves curvature unchanged.

label: The Surface Patch
notes: A regular patch is a smooth map of two parameters into space whose partial derivatives stay independent. Those two derivative vectors span the tangent plane at each point, and their cross product gives the unit normal. The sphere example shows why charts can fail at poles.

label: First Fundamental Form
notes: The first fundamental form is the dot product of tangent vectors written in the parameter coordinates. Its coefficients E, F, and G let us measure lengths of curves, angles between directions, and areas entirely from inside the surface, without ever referring to the ambient space.

label: Unit Normal and Second Form
notes: The unit normal points off the surface, and the second fundamental form measures how the surface pulls away from its tangent plane. Its coefficients L, M, and N come from dotting second derivatives of the patch with the normal, recording bending rather than intrinsic distance.

label: Normal Curvature
notes: Slice the surface with a plane containing the normal and a chosen tangent direction. The curvature of that section is the normal curvature, equal to the second form divided by the first in that direction. It is a ratio of two quadratic forms in the direction coefficients.

label: Principal Curvatures and Euler
notes: As the cutting direction rotates, normal curvature reaches a maximum and a minimum, the principal curvatures, along perpendicular principal directions. Euler's theorem expresses curvature in any direction as a cosine-squared blend of these two extremes, recovering every normal section from just two numbers.

label: Principal Directions as Eigenproblem
notes: Finding principal data is a generalized eigenvalue problem: the second form acting on a direction equals a curvature times the first form acting on it. The eigenvalues are the principal curvatures and the eigenvectors are the principal directions, automatically orthogonal in the surface metric.

label: Gaussian and Mean Curvature
notes: From the two principal curvatures we form two symmetric combinations. Gaussian curvature is their product and equals the ratio of the two form determinants. Mean curvature is their average. Gaussian curvature classifies local shape, while mean curvature governs minimal surfaces and soap films.

label: Sign of K Classifies Shape
notes: The sign of Gaussian curvature sorts every surface point into three types. Positive curvature gives a bowl that stays on one side of its tangent plane, zero gives a flat or developable direction, and negative gives a saddle that crosses its tangent plane along two directions.

label: Three Model Surfaces
notes: The sphere has constant positive curvature everywhere, the cylinder has zero curvature because one principal curvature vanishes, and the saddle has negative curvature with principal curvatures of opposite sign. These three pictures anchor every later statement about how surfaces bend in space.

label: Theorema Egregium
notes: Gauss's remarkable theorem states that Gaussian curvature, though defined using the ambient normal, can be computed from the first fundamental form alone. Curvature is therefore intrinsic and survives any bending that preserves distances, which is why flat paper cannot wrap a sphere without distortion.

label: Umbilics and Dupin's Indicatrix
notes: At an umbilic the two principal curvatures coincide, so every direction is principal and the surface looks locally spherical. The Dupin indicatrix is the tangent-plane conic that encodes all normal curvatures at a point, an ellipse, hyperbola pair, or parallel lines by sign.

label: Dupin and Liouville
notes: Dupin's theorem says three mutually orthogonal families of surfaces cut lines of curvature on one another, giving curvature-line coordinates for free. Liouville's theorem says angle-preserving maps of space send spheres to spheres, with planes counted as spheres through infinity, modeled by inversion.

label: Recap
notes: We assembled a complete local toolkit: the first form measures intrinsic distance, the second form measures bending, their interplay yields principal and Gaussian curvature, and Theorema Egregium makes that curvature an invariant of the surface itself rather than of any particular embedding in space.
